etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French entrance (“entry”). Replaced native Middle English ingang (“entrance, admission”), from Old English ingang (“ingress, entry, entrance”).

definitions.definition: (countable) The action of entering, or going in.
The act of taking possession, as of property, or of office.
(countable) The place of entering, as a gate or doorway.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 1, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: ‘It was called the wickedest street in London and the entrance was just here. I imagine the mouth of the road lay between this lamp standard and the second from the next down there.’

definitions.definition: The entering upon; the beginning, or that with which the beginning is made; the commencement; initiation.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Beware of entrance to a quarrel.
in the entrance of the history of this great patriarch

definitions.definition: The causing to be entered upon a register, as a ship or goods, at a customhouse; an entering.
(nautical) The angle which the bow of a vessel makes with the water at the water line.

quote.text: A coarse-lined ship, fig. 4, has an angle of entrance of about 40 deg., measured at the load-water line; while a fine-lined ship has only about half that angle.

quote.citation: 1919, Shipbuilding and Shipping Record - Volume 13, page 667:
quote.text: At low , say 9 knots for a 400-ft. ship, 60 deg. entrance angle (side to side) can be accepted.

quote.citation: 2018, A. Marinò, V. Bucci, Technology and Science for the Ships of the Future, page 788:
quote.text: This bulb therefore creates a greater wave but has a higher form resistance as the waterlines have larger entrance angles.

definitions.definition: (nautical) The bow, or entire wedgelike forepart of a vessel, below the water line.

quote.text: She [the Albemarle] has a bold entrance, and clean run.

definitions.definition: (music) The beginning of a musician's playing or singing; entry.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From en- + trance (“daze”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To delight and fill with wonder.

quote.citation: 1996, Tab Murphy, Irene Mecchi, Bob Tzudiker, Noni White, and Jonathan Roberts, The Hunchback of Notre Dame (film)
quote.text: See the finest girl in France make an entrance to entrance...
